documents.unit: The Institute for Learning and Teaching (TILT), Academic Integrity
documents.title: NavigateAI Use at CSU: What's allowed, When to ask, and What to avoid
documents.summary: A student-facing trail-map guide that sorts AI uses into three zones: always acceptable learning uses, uses that need the instructor's explicit permission, and uses that count as academic misconduct. The instructor decides what is allowed for credit work, and an FAQ section restates that help rules vary by course.
documents.stance_why: The page sets three tiers ("Some paths are open to everyone, some require special permits, and some are closed") and says "Using AI for any work you get credit for requires their explicit permission," with "Every guide runs their trail differently." The decision for graded work is handed to each instructor, so the document delegates and lists its tiers.

units.why: The opening sorts AI use into open, permit-required and closed paths: "Some paths are open to everyone, some require special permits, and some are closed". That is a named-tier scheme, so P05; it states no rule itself, so it informs.
units.anchor: Some paths are open to everyone, some require special permits, and some are closed
units.frag_start: Some paths are open to everyone,

units.why: "You are encouraged to use AI as your personal guide for learning and discovery" welcomes AI for learning in the open zone. It fits the tutor-for-understanding type P12 (not P02, which is a default for graded work) but is broader than a tutor, hence the fit note.
units.anchor: You are encouraged to use AI as your personal guide for learning and discovery.
units.fit_note: Encourages AI as a guide for learning and discovery in general, not only as a concept tutor.

units.why: "Use AI to explain a complex topic from class in a new way" is an always-acceptable use: AI as a tutor for understanding concepts, so P12.
units.anchor: Use AI to explain a complex topic from class in a new way.

units.why: "Explore concepts related to your course" with a list of key figures or debates is exploring a subject with AI, not producing graded answers. That is the tutor/search-engine use in P12.
units.anchor: Explore concepts related to your course.

units.why: "Create practice questions or flashcards to study for an exam" is a listed always-acceptable study aid, so P14.
units.anchor: Create practice questions or flashcards to study for an exam.

units.why: "AI tools can sometimes lead you astray with wrong information (hallucinations)" and "You are always responsible for verifying the facts and the quality of your work" tell students to check AI output, so P31 (not P29, since the point is verifying AI output).
units.anchor: You are always responsible for verifying the facts and the quality of your work.
units.policy: Students are always responsible for verifying the facts and the quality of their work, because AI tools can give wrong information (hallucinations).

units.why: "Using AI for any work you get credit for requires their explicit permission" sets a default that AI on credit work is off unless the instructor permits it. That is a ban-unless-permitted default, nearest P01; P06 is about syllabus silence, which is not the point here.
units.anchor: Using AI for any work you get credit for requires their explicit permission.
units.fit_note: Default is permission-required rather than an outright ban on graded work.

units.why: "Getting a permit means asking your instructor if, and how, you can use AI for a specific assignment" makes permission a per-assignment instructor decision, so P04.
units.anchor: asking your instructor if, and how, you can use AI for a specific assignment

units.why: "Every guide runs their trail differently" says instructors set different AI rules. It is a statement that rules vary by instructor, so P04 with modality informs.
units.anchor: Every guide runs their trail differently.

units.why: "Write or co-author any part of a graded essay, lab report, or paper" is listed under uses to check with the instructor first. It is a writing-specific permission-required rule, so P18 (prose separate from code).
units.anchor: Write or co-author any part of a graded essay, lab report, or paper.
units.policy: Students check with their instructor before using AI to write or co-author any part of a graded essay, lab report, or paper.

units.why: "Outline or organize your arguments for a graded assignment" also needs instructor permission first. It concerns prose planning, so P18; P91 is the permission itself, which is not what is given here.
units.anchor: Outline or organize your arguments for a graded assignment.
units.policy: Students check with their instructor before using AI to outline or organize their arguments for a graded assignment.

units.why: "Generate code or solve problems for credit" is on the list to check with the instructor before using AI. It is code generation that is allowed only with permission, nearest P16, but P16 lists conditions of use and here the condition is only instructor approval.
units.anchor: Generate code or solve problems for credit.
units.policy: Students check with their instructor before using AI to generate code or solve problems for credit.
units.fit_note: Permission is conditional only on prior instructor approval; no stated limits on size or citation.

units.why: "Complete any portion of a take-home quiz, exam, or assignment" needs instructor permission first. It is about take-home assessments, so P22 fits only partly (P22 is a ban on exams).
units.anchor: Complete any portion of a take-home quiz, exam, or assignment.
units.policy: Students check with their instructor before using AI to complete any portion of a take-home quiz, exam, or assignment.
units.fit_note: Take-home assessments are allowed with instructor permission, not banned outright.

units.why: "When in doubt, ask your guide" is the "#1 Rule of the Trail": students unsure whether an AI use is allowed should ask the instructor, so P10.
units.anchor: The #1 Rule of the Trail: When in doubt, ask your guide.

units.why: "An unauthorized trip here is considered academic misconduct" classifies unauthorized AI use in the permit zone as misconduct, so P36.
units.anchor: An unauthorized trip here is considered academic misconduct.

units.why: "Entering it is a violation of CSU's Academic Integrity Policy" and the rule "applies to anything considered 'work for credit'" define the scope of the closed zone and tie it to the integrity policy. It defines scope, so P61 (P36 would be the misconduct label, already coded above).
units.anchor: This applies to anything considered “work for credit” (graded, pass/fail, or marked as completed).
units.fit_note: Defines scope as work for credit rather than defining AI itself.

units.why: "Turning in an essay, lab report, or any other assignment that was fully generated by an AI" is listed as misconduct. It is a ban on submitting AI-produced work, so P19.
units.anchor: any other assignment that was fully generated by an AI.

units.why: "Using an AI tool in any way to answer questions during a quiz or exam" is misconduct: a ban on AI in exams, so P22.
units.anchor: Using an AI tool in any way to answer questions during a quiz or exam.

units.why: "Including fake sources, data, or citations that an AI made up" is misconduct. It forbids submitting fabricated material that AI produced, which is closest to P74 (fabricate or falsify data); P31 only tells students to verify.
units.anchor: Including fake sources, data, or citations that an AI made up
units.fit_note: Concerns AI-fabricated sources in the student's own submission, not intent to deceive by the tool user in general.

units.why: "Using AI to rewrite or 'spin' sentences or paragraphs from a source and presenting them as your own original summary" is misconduct. AI is producing text submitted as one's own, so P19.
units.anchor: Using AI to rewrite or “spin” sentences or paragraphs from a source

units.why: "Intentionally hiding your use of AI on an assignment where your instructor has explicitly asked you to declare it" makes nondisclosure itself the violation, so P28.
units.anchor: Intentionally hiding your use of AI on an assignment

units.why: "Submitting AI-generated code, formulas, or solutions and claiming them as your own work" is misconduct. It bans passing off AI-generated code as one's own, so P19.
units.anchor: Submitting AI-generated code, formulas, or solutions and claiming them

units.why: The helicopter analogy says "building the strength and skill that only come from the climb (the learning process)" is the goal of an assignment. It explains the ban by skill-building, so P41.
units.anchor: building the strength and skill that only come from the climb

units.why: "How do I credit my AI Tools (when allowed)? Visit the CSU Library's AI Citation Guide" points students to a citation guide when AI use is permitted, so a disclosure-by-citation pointer, P24.
units.anchor: How do I credit my AI Tools (when allowed)?
units.policy: When AI use is allowed, students credit their AI tools following the CSU Library's AI Citation Guide.
units.fit_note: A pointer to a library citation guide; it does not itself require a statement.

units.why: "The content and framework were developed by the CSU Academic Integrity Program. We used a large language model as a collaborative partner" states who made the guide and how, so P84.
units.anchor: The content and framework were developed by the CSU Academic Integrity Program.
units.fit_note: Also discloses the authors' own LLM use in drafting.

units.why: "The simple answer is the instructor. Because the instructor of a course decides what is acceptable and unacceptable help, the expectation can change from course to course." Instructors set the help rules, so P04.
units.anchor: the instructor of a course decides what is acceptable and unacceptable help
units.policy: The instructor of a course decides what is acceptable and unacceptable help on an assignment, essay, or exam, so the expectation can change from course to course.
units.fit_note: Stated for help in general, not AI specifically; it frames the AI rules above.

units.why: The example "you may be allowed to work with a partner at every step of an assignment in one class, and not allowed to collaborate at all in another" shows rules do not carry between courses, so P11.
units.anchor: allowed to work with a partner at every step of an assignment
units.fit_note: Example is about partner collaboration, not AI.

documents.unit: The Institute for Learning and Teaching (TILT)
documents.title: Crafting Syllabus Statements on Generative Artificial Intelligence Use
tiers: A Statement Allowing Limited & Guided Use
A Permissive Statement Focused on Accountability
documents.summary: Faculty guide to writing short course AI statements, with four sample statements ranging from prohibitive to broadly permissive. It argues that a campus-wide umbrella policy is unlikely to fit and asks instructors to use their own judgment and update their statements.
documents.stance_why: The guide offers four adoptable sample statements and says "it seems unlikely that a campus umbrella policy will satisfy the many needs" and "You are urged to use your best judgment." It sets no university-wide AI rule and hands the decision to instructors, so it delegates with tiers.

units.why: "Students should immediately understand whether they are allowed to use AI and how they are allowed to use it" says every course statement must make the AI rule plain, so P09.
units.anchor: Students should immediately understand whether they are allowed to use AI

units.why: "They exist for administrative reasons: when something undesirable occurs ... they are what we point to as the stated expectation of the course" explains why a statement is needed, supporting P09 as the reason for stating expectations; it does not itself require one.
units.anchor: they are what we point to as the stated expectation of the course
units.fit_note: Explains that statements serve as the basis for intervening in misconduct, not an obligation to write one.

units.why: "What is the scope of the policy? Does it cover all course activities or only graded work?" tells instructors a statement should say what it covers, so P09 (stating expectations in the syllabus).
units.anchor: Does it cover all course activities or only graded work?
units.policy: An ideal AI syllabus statement answers what the scope of the policy is, including whether it covers all course activities or only graded work.

units.why: "State clearly what students are allowed and not allowed to do" tells instructors to spell out permitted and prohibited uses in the statement, so P09.
units.anchor: State clearly what students are allowed and not allowed to do.

units.why: "If you plan to use a clarifying resource, a color-coded chart or other guide, reference it here" lets instructors use a tiered framework and name it in the statement, so P05.
units.anchor: a color-coded chart or other guide, reference it here
units.policy: Instructors who use a clarifying resource such as a color-coded chart or other guide reference it in the syllabus statement.

units.why: "Encourage dialogue by inviting students to talk with you" asks instructors to open a conversation with students about the AI rule, so P66.
units.anchor: Encourage dialogue by inviting students to talk with you.

units.why: "The right statement for your course will depend on your specific learning objectives" ties the AI rule to course goals, so P83.
units.anchor: The right statement for your course will depend on your specific learning
units.policy: The right AI syllabus statement for a course depends on that course's specific learning objectives.

units.why: The sample "You may NOT use AI when completing any assignments, assessments, or other work for credit in this course" is a model ban on AI for credit work, so P01. Offered as an adoptable option, not a rule of the university.
units.anchor: You may NOT use AI when completing any assignments, assessments, or other work for credit
units.frag_end: work for credit in this course.

units.why: In the same sample, "You MAY use it to investigate, study, summarize, etc. course material, concepts" keeps a study-use exception under the ban. That is AI as a tool for understanding and review; P12 fits (P14 also lists summaries), and I chose P12 as the lead use is investigating concepts.
units.anchor: You MAY use it to investigate, study, summarize, etc. course material, concepts, etc.

units.why: The conditional sample says "You may only use generative AI in this class in specific ways" and points to a color-coded framework showing how and when. That sets a tiered scheme, so P05.
units.anchor: I will use a color-coded framework to make it clear HOW you can use AI

units.why: "we will discuss how you may use AI on each course assignment or assessment at the time it is introduced" makes AI permission an assignment-by-assignment decision, so P04.
units.anchor: we will discuss how you may use AI on each course assignment or assessment

units.why: "You are not authorized to use artificial intelligence to produce work for this class except on assignments that I have explicitly identified" bans AI unless permitted for named assignments, a ban-by-default with listed exceptions, so P01 (the exception list is coded separately below).
units.anchor: You are not authorized to use artificial intelligence to produce work for this class
units.policy: Students are not authorized to use artificial intelligence to produce work for the class except on assignments the instructor has explicitly identified, where they receive significant guidance on appropriate use.
units.fit_note: Ban with exceptions only on assignments the instructor identifies, plus guided use.

units.why: "You may not construe this limited permission as approval to use these technologies in any other facet of this course" says permission for one assignment does not extend elsewhere, so P11.
units.anchor: You may not construe this limited permission as approval to use these technologies
units.fit_note: Limits permission to identified assignments within the same course rather than across courses.

units.why: "The use of generative AI tools is broadly permitted in this course to help you brainstorm, draft, and revise your work" is a permit-by-default sample, so P02.
units.anchor: broadly permitted in this course to help you brainstorm, draft, and revise

units.why: "You are fully accountable for the final submission" in the permissive sample makes students responsible for what they hand in, so P29.
units.anchor: authentic engagement means you are fully accountable for the final submission

units.why: "Fact-check all AI-generated content for accuracy" is a requirement to verify AI output, so P31.
units.anchor: Fact-check all AI-generated content for accuracy.

units.why: "Revise all content to ensure it meets assignment requirements and reflects your own understanding" requires students to make AI output their own. P29 (own work) is nearer than P32 because it concerns the submitted product, not who solves the problem.
units.anchor: Revise all content to ensure it meets assignment requirements and reflects your own understanding
units.fit_note: Requires revision of AI content so it reflects the student's own understanding.

units.why: "Cite your use of the AI tool following the guidance in the CSU Library's Guidelines for Acknowledging AI Use in Research" requires citing AI use, so P24.
units.anchor: Cite your use of the AI tool following the guidance in the
units.policy: Students cite their use of the AI tool following the CSU Library's Guidelines for Acknowledging AI Use in Research.

units.why: "Submitting inaccurate or unedited AI-generated work fails to meet the standards for academic integrity and will result in a poor grade" states a consequence for unverified AI work. P37 is the nearest type, but the penalty is only "a poor grade", hence the fit note.
units.anchor: will result in a poor grade
units.policy: Submitting inaccurate or unedited AI-generated work fails to meet the standards for academic integrity and will result in a poor grade.
units.fit_note: The penalty is only a poor grade, tied to inaccurate or unedited work, not a scale of penalties.

units.why: "Generative AI provides an opportunity to foster the key literacies" frames AI literacy as something faculty build into courses, so P70 (curricular AI literacy).
units.anchor: Faculty can emphasize these literacies to help students engage with AI tools

units.why: "Teach students how to use generative AI tools effectively, gaining fluency in their features and applications" asks faculty to teach effective AI use as a skill, so P44.
units.anchor: Teach students how to use generative AI tools effectively, gaining fluency
units.fit_note: Framed as functional literacy, with no mention of employers.

units.why: "Encourage students to evaluate AI's strengths, weaknesses, assumptions, and societal impacts" asks faculty to build critical evaluation of AI. P31 is nearest (evaluate AI critically), though it also reaches societal impacts.
units.anchor: Encourage students to evaluate AI’s strengths, weaknesses, assumptions, and societal impacts
units.fit_note: Also includes assumptions and societal impacts, beyond verifying correctness.

units.why: "Guide students to assess when and how to use AI in different contexts, emphasizing audience, purpose" is rhetorical AI literacy taught in courses, with no matching specific type, so P70 (curricular AI literacy).
units.anchor: Guide students to assess when and how to use AI in different contexts

units.why: "raises valid concerns about academic integrity and critical thinking, environmental impact, unevenly distributed access" names harms and concerns of AI, so P53 (access is a part of that sentence, but the sentence is mainly a list of concerns).
units.anchor: environmental impact, unevenly distributed access
units.fit_note: Also names academic integrity, critical thinking and unequal access.

units.why: "it seems unlikely that a campus umbrella policy will satisfy the many needs and concerns" because AI's usefulness "will vary widely"; the university leaves AI rules to individual courses, so P04.
units.anchor: it seems unlikely that a campus umbrella policy will satisfy the many needs and concerns

units.why: "You are urged to use your best judgment and to update your syllabus languages your ideas change" asks instructors to revise their statements over time, so P54.
units.anchor: to update your syllabus languages your ideas change
units.policy: Instructors are urged to use their best judgment and to update their syllabus language as their ideas change.

units.why: "Consider consulting the standards of your disciplinary community as a resource" points instructors to discipline-level norms for setting AI rules. No existing type covers using disciplinary standards, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Consider consulting the standards of your disciplinary community as a resource
units.uncovered_note: Instructors should consult their disciplinary community's standards when deciding their course AI rules.

units.why: The suggested question "How am I ensuring that the use of AI in my course promotes ... higher order thinking and learning" asks instructors to check their AI rule against learning goals, so P83 (fits partly; it is a prompt for reflection rather than a rule).
units.anchor: How am I ensuring that the use of AI in my course promotes an approach
units.fit_note: A reflective question about higher-order thinking rather than a stated link to objectives.

units.why: "This resource was coauthored using generative AI (Ram-GPT) under the guidance of Colorado State University employees" with "human review" states how the guide was made, so P84.
units.anchor: This resource was coauthored using generative AI (Ram-GPT) under the guidance
units.fit_note: Discloses the authors' own use of AI in drafting.

documents.title: Policies & Resources (Academic Integrity section)
documents.summary: The department's student information guide lists behaviors that are clearly unacceptable in CS coursework, and one of them is turning in generative-AI work as one's own. No permitted AI uses are described.
documents.stance_why: The only AI text is a bullet under "Examples of clearly unacceptable behaviors": "Turning in work created by generative AI as one's own." It bans submitting AI-created work as one's own and names no allowed uses or instructor discretion, so the stance is prohibit for that work.

units.why: Under "Examples of clearly unacceptable behaviors" the department lists "Turning in work created by generative AI as one's own." That bans submitting AI-created work, so P19; it is also labelled unacceptable (P36), but the rule a reader would look for is the ban on submitting AI work.
units.anchor: Turning in work created by generative AI as one’s own.

notes: CS department page has a single AI bullet; its general integrity rules (must be able to explain your solution, penalties list, duty to report to the Office of Conflict Resolution and Student Conduct Services) do not mention AI and were not coded. Navigate AI page text repeats its three zones twice; repeats were coded once. Non-AI FAQ items (Course Hero, double submission, facilitation) were skipped. The navigate page's 'Undeclared use' line is coded P28.
